saereg: SAE regression

Treatments and group differences often change texts in several ways at once. SAE regression estimates such an effect on texts and decomposes it into interpretable directions:

  1. Embed the texts with a language model (embed_texts()).
  2. Learn directions with a sparse autoencoder (SAE) trained on one half of the texts (train_sae()).
  3. Label the directions with a large language model, from the training texts that score highest on them (label_features()).
  4. Estimate and decompose on the other half (saereg()): the effect on the average text, a global test, and, for each direction, how far the texts move towards or away from it and what share of the effect it explains.

saereg() works like a regression. Covariates, absorbed fixed effects and clustered designs (e.g. difference-in-differences) are supported.

Installation 

# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("ElisaWirsching/saereg")

saereg() needs only R. Steps 1 to 3 run the package’s Python stages (inst/python/saereg_ml) and need a Python with numpy, pandas, pyarrow, pyyaml, torch, hypothesaes, tiktoken and openai:

options(saereg.python = "/path/to/python3")   # or set the environment variable SAEREG_PYTHON

Embedding and labeling call the OpenAI API: they need a key in the environment variable OPENAI_KEY_SAE and cost money. With dry_run = TRUE they show what they would send without sending it.

Example

The package ships the open-ended answers of a survey experiment on immigration and punishment (Egami et al. 2022), with their embeddings and an SAE trained on the training half.

library(saereg)
d <- egami$data
E <- egami$E
test <- !d$train

fit <- saereg(E[test, ] ~ treat, data = d[test, ], W = egami$W, labels = egami$labels)
fit              # the overall effect: squared norm, bias-corrected, global test, R^2
summary(fit)     # the directions by their share of the effect
confint(fit)     # effects along the directions, with jackknife intervals

The getting-started article walks through all four steps, with outputs; in R, vignette("getting_started", package = "saereg"). Documentation: https://elisawirsching.github.io/saereg/.

Citation

Wirsching, E. M. (2026). What moved? Interpretable decompositions of effects on text with sparse autoencoders. Working paper.

Licence and data

GPL-3. The example data come from the replication data of Egami, Fong, Grimmer, Roberts and Stewart (2022), “How to make causal inferences using texts”, Science Advances 8, Harvard Dataverse, doi:10.7910/DVN/QHJN8V (CC0 1.0).
